title: a fallible arrow handed to Array.prototype.map owes a Result contract like any other callback argument
notes: specification/failures.mdx, 'Inference and Public Contracts': 'Public, abstract, ambient, and declaration-only contracts MUST express fallibility directly with `Result<A, E>` or `Promise<Result<A, E>>`.' A callback boundary is a VALUE edge, not an argument position: the callee invokes a function it received inside an object literal, an array literal, a parenthesis, a cast or a `new` argument list exactly as it invokes one passed directly. Fail-closed matters here because the accepting behaviour is silent and wrong rather than loud and wrong — R1FIX executed this class before the fix and measured `isOk() === true` with a `Result` sitting in the SUCCESS payload, with zero language diagnostics and zero emitted-TypeScript diagnostics. `.map(() => lookup("ada")!)` is the shape an author reaches for first, and it is the shape where accepting silently is worst: the propagation returns from the CALLBACK, not from the enclosing function, so the failure never reaches the author's declared channel and the array is populated with Results. Until 2026-08-25 the reference accepted this program, precisely because the abolished `!` meaning manufactured an inferred Result contract that silenced the rule — the same cause as a-propagating-callback-needs-a-contract-even-though-its-inferred-type-is-a-result, in the most ordinary spelling. Both backends now report SMITHERS1303 here. RETIRED XFAIL (go): the fork reported the declared SMITHERS1303@11:29 correctly and ADDED SMITHERS1204@11:35 for the `!` in the concise arrow body — a diagnostics case is exact in both directions, so an extra true-in-spirit diagnostic was still a divergence. It was one defect with 02-unwrap-propagation/postfix-bang-in-a-concise-arrow-body-is-accepted and retired in the same edit: `safeUnwrapPlacement` treated an arrow function as a rejection where 'Accepted Placements' condition 1 makes it a STOP, and `lowerConciseBody` now synthesises the block body such a placement needs. Nothing about the SMITHERS1303 rule this case exists to pin was touched; the row that moved is the one that should never have been there.
